claims.text: A physics-informed machine-learning framework can rapidly and accurately predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness for hierarchical-heterostructured HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework will significantly reduce computational demand relative to high-fidelity CALPHAD and full first-principles methods.
HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure exhibiting multilevel chemical fluctuations.
Elastic constants, misfit volumes, surface energies, and unstable stacking-fault energies are suitable surrogate descriptors for this prediction task.
A model trained on a curated dataset of related HEAs can generalize to hierarchical-heterostructured HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed predictions apply at room temperature and moderate elevated temperatures while the hierarchical structure remains stable.
The surrogate descriptors capture the alloy’s multilevel chemical fluctuations and phase heterogeneities.
Captured chemical fluctuations and phase heterogeneities mediate the relationship between microstructure and macroscopic mechanical response.
Encoding physical relationships in surrogate descriptors reduces the parameter space that would otherwise require expensive simulations.
The reduced parameter space enables faster convergence toward accurate elastic and fracture-property predictions.
The hybrid model will predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness within ±10% of experimental values.
The hybrid model will reduce computational cost by approximately 50–70% relative to CALPHAD or full first-principles methods.
Existing CALPHAD and full first-principles methods typically have predictive variability of approximately ±20% or more.
Ab initio methods are time-consuming and CALPHAD can require significant computational resources for HEA prediction.
Machine-learning prediction accuracy for HEAs can exceed 90%, but is sensitive to the size and composition of the training dataset.
The model may cease to be reliable when unexpected phase transformations or microstructural rearrangements occur under extreme temperature or loading.
The model may cease to be reliable outside its training regime when the selected descriptors omit relevant physics.
The benchmark will compare model predictions with measured Young’s modulus, tensile yield strength, and fracture toughness for synthesized HfNbTiVAl10.
Prediction errors greater than ±10% across multiple trials will falsify the accuracy hypothesis.
Computational savings below 50% relative to CALPHAD or first-principles approaches will falsify the efficiency hypothesis.
